690:
Amplitude means how far something swings away from its resting, neutral position — and by extension, it's a measure of the size, intensity, or extent of something.

Think of it like this: if you push a child on a swing and let go, the swing will travel back and forth. The amplitude is how far the swing travels from the very center point — not the total distance from one end to the other, but the distance from the middle to its farthest point in either direction.

That's the single most important thing to understand about amplitude. It is always measured from the center outward, not from one extreme to the other.
Amplitude in Waves (The Most Common Use)

This is where the word does most of its work. Almost everywhere you encounter "amplitude," it will be in the context of waves — sound waves, light waves, water waves, radio waves, and so on.

A wave, regardless of its type, has a characteristic shape. Imagine drawing a wavy line across a page: it goes up (that peak is called the crest), comes back to the middle, goes down (that dip is called the trough), and comes back to the middle again. This middle horizontal line represents the equilibrium — the resting, undisturbed state.

Amplitude is the distance from that equilibrium line to the very top of a crest (or equally, to the very bottom of a trough).

A few things to be precise about:

  • The amplitude from the center to the crest and from the center to the trough are always equal in a standard wave.
  • The total distance from crest to trough (top to bottom) is twice the amplitude. This is sometimes called the peak-to-peak amplitude, and it's a different measurement. When someone says "amplitude" without any qualifier, they mean the one-sided measurement from center to peak.
  • Amplitude is always a positive number because it is a measure of size/distance, and distances cannot be negative.

Amplitude is not just a geometric description — it tells you something deeply physical: how much energy the wave is carrying.

A wave with a large amplitude carries more energy. A wave with a small amplitude carries less energy. The energy in a wave is proportional to the square of its amplitude — so if you double the amplitude, the energy quadruples.

This shows up in everyday experience:

Sound waves: The amplitude of a sound wave determines its loudness. When a drummer hits a drum hard, the surface vibrates with greater amplitude, pushing the surrounding air harder, creating a loud sound. A soft tap creates small-amplitude vibrations — a quiet sound. Your ears detect amplitude and interpret it as volume.

Light and other electromagnetic waves: The amplitude of a light wave determines its brightness (intensity). A brighter light source is one whose waves have greater amplitude. Similarly, a more intense X-ray beam has higher-amplitude waves.

Water waves: The amplitude of an ocean wave tells you how tall the wave is. A calm sea has low-amplitude waves. A storm produces high-amplitude waves that carry enormous energy — enough to move ships, erode cliffs, and cause damage onshore.
Amplitude Is Not the Same as Frequency or Wavelength

This distinction trips up a lot of learners, so let's be very clear.

Frequency is how many times a wave completes a full cycle per second — in other words, how often it oscillates. A high-frequency sound is a high-pitched sound (like a whistle). A low-frequency sound is a low-pitched sound (like a bass drum). Frequency has nothing to do with how loud the sound is.

Wavelength is the physical distance between two consecutive crests (or two consecutive troughs) — in other words, how long one full cycle is.

Amplitude is how tall the wave is — how far it deviates from equilibrium.

These three are completely independent of each other. You can have:

  • A wave that is high in frequency but low in amplitude (a quiet high-pitched beep)
  • A wave that is low in frequency but high in amplitude (a very loud bass rumble)
  • Any other combination

Think of it this way: if you're watching ocean waves from above, wavelength is the distance between the crests, frequency is how many crests pass a fixed point per second, and amplitude is how high each crest rises above calm water. Same wave, three different measurements, three different things.

Outside of science, "amplitude" is used as a somewhat formal or literary word to mean largeness, breadth, abundance, or fullness of scope. It conveys that something is wide-ranging or substantial.

For example:

  • "The amplitude of her knowledge on the subject was remarkable" — meaning the sheer breadth and depth of her knowledge.
  • "He spoke with amplitude and confidence" — meaning his speech was full, expansive, and unhurried.
  • "The amplitude of the problem became clear only over time" — meaning the full scale and extent of the problem.

In this usage, it's more of a stylistic word that implies magnitude and generousness of extent. It's rarely used this way in everyday casual speech — you're much more likely to encounter it in writing, literature, or formal contexts.

You may have seen "AM" on a radio dial. AM stands for Amplitude Modulation. This is a technique where audio information (a voice, music) is encoded into a radio wave by continuously varying its amplitude in sync with the audio signal. The frequency of the carrier wave stays the same; only the amplitude changes. Your radio detects those amplitude changes and converts them back into sound. This is a perfect, practical example of amplitude at work.

ContextWhat amplitude measures

In everyday language: amplitude means largeness, fullness, or extent.

In science: amplitude is the maximum displacement of a wave from its equilibrium (rest) position. It is measured from the center to the peak — not from peak to trough. It tells you how much energy a wave carries. For sound, it determines loudness. For light, it determines brightness and intensity. For water, it tells you the height of the wave.

It is separate from, and independent of, both frequency (how fast the wave oscillates) and wavelength (the physical length of one cycle).

The word always points toward the idea of how big, how full, how far — whether describing a wave, a voice, or a body of knowledge.
691:
Amply means in a way that is more than enough — generously, fully, and with room to spare.

It is the adverb form of the adjective "ample," which means "more than sufficient." When you add the "-ly" ending to make it an adverb, it describes how something is done — specifically, that it is done to a generous, satisfying degree.

Think of it this way: imagine filling a glass with water.

  • Filling it just barely to the brim = enough
  • Filling it so well that it's clearly, comfortably full, with no doubt about it = amply
  • Overflowing it carelessly = too much / excessively

Amply lives in that second space — generously sufficient, beyond any doubt.

The word carries a quiet sense of confirmation or reassurance. When you say something was done amply, you're not just saying it was done enough — you're saying it was done so well that the matter is settled. There is no room for doubt or complaint. This is what separates "amply" from a plain word like "enough."

Compare:

  • "She was paid enough." → She got what was required. Nothing more, nothing less.
  • "She was amply rewarded." → She was rewarded generously, more than sufficiently, in a way that clearly matched or exceeded what she deserved.

The second sentence feels richer, more final, more certain.

Amply is a slightly formal word. You will find it more often in writing — news articles, academic papers, books, formal reports — than in casual spoken conversation. Everyday speakers are more likely to say "more than enough," "well," or "fully" in speech. But in writing, "amply" is elegant and precise.

As an adverb, amply describes:

Verbs — it tells you how an action was carried out.

"The study amply demonstrates that exercise improves mood."
(The study shows it generously and convincingly — there is no doubt left.)

"He was amply compensated for his hard work."
(He was paid generously, more than just fairly.)

Adjectives — it tells you to what degree something is true.

"She is amply qualified for the role."
(She has qualifications in full measure — clearly, comfortably enough and then some.)

"The room was amply large for the meeting."
(The room had more than enough space — no one felt cramped.)

Certain words pair with "amply" so often that you should learn them as natural combinations:

  • Amply demonstrated / amply shown / amply illustrated — used when evidence or proof is strong and abundant. "The data amply demonstrates the link between the two."
  • Amply rewarded / amply compensated — used when payment, praise, or recognition is generous. "Their patience was amply rewarded."
  • Amply justified — used when a decision or action is very well supported by reasons. "Her caution was amply justified by what happened next."
  • Amply supported — used when an argument, claim, or person has strong backing. "The theory is amply supported by historical evidence."
  • Amply qualified / amply suited — used when someone has more than enough skills or qualities. "He was amply suited to lead the team."

These pairings are the natural home of the word. If you learn to use it in these contexts first, you will sound natural and correct.

Here are several sentences showing the word at work across different situations:

  1. "The documentary amply captured the suffering of those affected by the disaster."

(It captured it fully, convincingly, and without any shortcoming.)

  1. "Her years of experience amply prepared her for the challenges ahead."

(Her experience gave her more than enough preparation.)

  1. "The fundraiser amply exceeded its goal, raising twice the expected amount."

(It surpassed the goal generously, not just barely.)

  1. "The book's success was amply deserved."

(The success was fully and rightly earned — in clear and generous measure.)

  1. "The resources provided were amply sufficient to complete the project."

(There was more than enough — no shortage, no doubt.)

This is important to get right:

  • It does not mean "excessively" or "too much." If someone ate too much food, you would not say they amply ate — you would say they overate or ate excessively.
  • It does not mean "barely" or "just about." It is always on the generous side, not the thin side.
  • It does not mean "simply" or "easily" — don't confuse it with words like "simply" or "merely."

These words are close to "amply" but each has a slightly different shade:

  • Sufficiently — means "enough," but feels neutral and minimal. Amply is warmer and more generous.
  • Fully — means completely. Amply adds the extra idea of generous completeness.
  • Generously — focuses on the spirit of giving. Amply focuses more on the amount or degree.
  • Abundantly — very similar to amply, but stronger and more emphatic. "Abundantly clear" feels even more forceful than "amply clear."
  • Well — the most casual substitute. "Well demonstrated" means roughly the same as "amply demonstrated" but is less formal.

If you remember just one thing: amply means in a generous, more-than-enough way that leaves no room for doubt. It is the adverb you reach for when you want to say something was done fully, convincingly, and with plenty to spare.
692: To amputate means to surgically cut off a limb or body part from a person's (or animal's) body. It is a deliberate, controlled act — not an accident — almost always performed by a trained surgeon using medical tools while the patient is under anesthesia (so they feel no pain during the procedure).

The word is most commonly used for:

  • Major limbs — an entire arm or leg
  • Partial limbs — the lower half of a leg, a forearm, etc.
  • Extremities — a hand, foot, finger, or toe

Less commonly, it can refer to other protruding or attachable body parts, such as a breast in certain cancer surgeries, or even a tail in veterinary medicine.
Why Would a Doctor Amputate Something?

A doctor amputates a body part only when keeping it would be more dangerous than removing it. The most common reasons are:

  • Severe injury — a crushing accident, a battlefield wound, or a traumatic event so damaging that the limb cannot be saved or repaired.
  • Disease that kills tissue — conditions like gangrene (where tissue rots and dies due to lack of blood or infection) can spread to the rest of the body if the dead tissue is not removed.
  • Cancer — a tumour in a limb that cannot be treated any other way.
  • Diabetes complications — long-term diabetes can destroy blood circulation in the feet and legs, causing tissue to die.
  • Severe frostbite — extreme cold can kill tissue permanently, making removal necessary.

In every case, the goal of amputation is to save the patient's life or prevent the spread of a deadly condition.

A surgeon cuts through the skin, muscle, and bone at a specific point — chosen carefully to leave the healthiest possible tissue behind. The blood vessels are sealed to prevent bleeding, and the remaining skin is shaped and closed over the wound to form what is called a stump — the remaining end of the limb. This stump can later be fitted with an artificial limb (called a prosthetic).

FormExample
Amputates (3rd person)The surgeon amputates the leg.
Amputated (past tense)They amputated his foot after the accident.
Amputating (present participle)The team is amputating the limb now.
Amputation (noun)The amputation was a success.
Amputee (noun — the person)She is an amputee who uses a prosthetic arm.

• Doctors had to amputate his right leg below the knee after the infection spread too far.
  • The surgeon decided to amputate the finger rather than risk the gangrene spreading.
  • Her arm was so severely crushed in the accident that the medical team had no choice but to amputate it.

In non-medical writing, "amputate" is sometimes used metaphorically to describe cutting something off decisively and permanently — especially when that thing was once an integral part of a larger whole.

  • The CEO decided to amputate the loss-making division from the company before it dragged everything else down.
  • He felt as though his past had been amputated from him — gone, with nothing but a scar left behind.

This figurative use works because it carries the emotional weight of the medical term: something permanent, drastic, and irreversible has been removed.
The Key Feeling of the Word

The most important thing to feel about this word is its weight and finality. You don't amputate something casually or temporarily. It is always:

  • Surgical and deliberate (not accidental)
  • Permanent (what is removed does not grow back)
  • Drastic (it is a last resort, not a first option)

This is what separates "amputate" from softer words like "remove" or "cut." When you use "amputate," you are signalling something serious, irreversible, and significant.
693:
An amulet is a small object that a person keeps or wears because they believe it has the magical power to protect them from harm, evil, bad luck, illness, or danger.

The key word here is believe. An amulet does not work the way a helmet protects your head or a lock protects your door. Its power is supernatural — meaning it belongs to the world of belief, magic, spirits, or religion, not science or mechanics. Whether an amulet actually works is a matter of personal faith, not proven fact.

Amulets have no fixed shape or material. They can be almost anything:

  • A carved stone or gemstone
  • A metal pendant worn on a necklace
  • A small pouch containing herbs, bones, or written prayers
  • A figurine or symbol
  • A piece of cloth inscribed with holy words
  • A specially shaped piece of wood or bone

What matters is not what it is made of, but what meaning people attach to it — the belief that the object carries a protective power.
What an Amulet Is Supposed to Do

An amulet's main job is protection. More specifically, it is meant to:

  • Repel evil — keep away evil spirits, curses, or dark forces
  • Ward off bad luck — prevent misfortune from reaching the wearer
  • Guard against illness or injury — protect physical well-being
  • Shield against the ill intentions of others — such as jealousy, hatred, or a curse placed by an enemy

Some amulets are also believed to attract good things — like luck, health, or love — though that role more precisely belongs to a related object called a talisman (see below).

Amulets are typically worn on the body — as a necklace, bracelet, ring, or pinned to clothing — so the protective power stays close to the person at all times. Some amulets are not worn but instead placed in specific locations: hung above a doorway, kept inside a home, buried under a threshold, or placed near a bed. The goal is always the same — to create a protected zone around a person or place.

People carry or wear amulets during moments of special vulnerability: before a battle, during childbirth, while traveling through dangerous lands, or when they fear someone has wished them ill.

Amulets have existed in virtually every culture in history. Some well-known examples:

  • The Nazar (Evil Eye charm) — a blue glass eye-shaped bead, widely used in Turkey, Greece, and across the Middle East. It is believed to protect the wearer from the "evil eye," which is the harm that a jealous or envious glare can cause.
  • The Scarab Beetle — used in ancient Egypt, believed to carry protective and life-giving power.
  • The Hamsa Hand — a palm-shaped symbol used across Middle Eastern and North African cultures to ward off evil.
  • The Ankh — an Egyptian cross-like symbol associated with life and protection.
  • Religious medallions — for example, a St. Christopher medal worn by Catholic travelers for protection on journeys.
  • A horseshoe hung above a door — a folk amulet believed to bring protection and keep evil from entering the home.
  • A rabbit's foot — a folk charm carried for protection and luck.
  • Crystals and gemstones — many people today wear specific stones (like black tourmaline or obsidian) believing they repel negative energy.
Amulet vs. Talisman — A Helpful Distinction

These two words are often used interchangeably in everyday speech, but there is a traditional and useful difference:

  • An amulet pushes bad things away — it protects, repels, and shields. It is defensive.
  • A talisman pulls good things toward you — it attracts fortune, power, love, or success. It is magnetic and active.

Think of it this way: an amulet is like a shield; a talisman is like a magnet. Many real-world objects serve both roles and get called by either name depending on who you ask — but in precise usage, amulet leans toward protection from harm.

Over time, the word "amulet" has also come to be used loosely and informally to describe anything — even a non-magical object — that a person treats as though it brings them protection or luck. A person might call a lucky pen they always carry to exams their "amulet," or a piece of jewelry from a loved one that makes them feel safe. In this loose sense, the word just means a personal object charged with sentimental or symbolic protective meaning, even without a belief in literal magic.
How to Use the Word in a Sentence

• She wore a small jade amulet around her neck to protect herself from evil spirits.
  • In many ancient cultures, soldiers carried amulets into battle, hoping they would survive unharmed.
  • The old woman sold handmade amulets at the market, each one carved with protective symbols.
  • He did not believe in magic, but he still kept his grandfather's coin as a kind of amulet — it made him feel safe.
An amulet is a small object believed to protect its wearer from harm, evil, bad luck, or danger through supernatural or magical power.
694:
To amuse someone means to cause them to feel gentle pleasure through something funny, entertaining, or pleasantly interesting. When something amuses you, a quiet smile crosses your face, or a soft chuckle escapes you. It is a light, warm feeling — not an overwhelming one.

Think of it this way: your friend tells a clever joke and you smile and laugh softly. You have been amused. A child makes a funny face and the adults in the room grin warmly. The child has amused them.

Sense 1 — To make someone laugh or smile
This is the most common use. Something or someone causes a gentle sense of humor or fun.

  • "The comedian's jokes amused the audience."
  • "His clumsy dancing amused his friends."
  • "The little girl amused everyone with her silly comments."

Sense 2 — To keep someone pleasantly occupied or entertained
Here, "amuse" means to fill someone's time in a way that keeps them happily engaged — not necessarily through humor, but through any pleasant activity that keeps boredom away.

  • "The teacher amused the children with a game."
  • "She amused herself by sketching portraits during the long train ride."
  • "The juggler amused the waiting crowd."

In this second sense, a child "amused" by a toy is simply happily busy with it.
The Feeling Is Light — Never Intense

This is one of the most important things to understand about "amuse." The feeling it produces is mild and gentle. It lives in the comfortable space between a quiet smile and a soft laugh.

Compare these words on a scale of intensity:

  • Amused → a gentle smile, a quiet chuckle, mild enjoyment
  • Pleased → a step up; happy and satisfied
  • Delighted → strong pleasure and happiness
  • Thrilled → very excited; intense positive feeling

So if something fills you with enormous joy or excitement, "amused" is too weak a word for it. But if something gives you a warm, easy smile? "Amused" is exactly right.

Both people and things can be the subject of "amuse":

  • A person can amuse: "She amused her guests with funny stories."
  • A thing can amuse: "The film amused me."
  • A situation or event can amuse: "The mix-up amused everyone present."

The person or thing that does the amusing is the subject; the person who feels the amusement is the object.

"Amuse" is very commonly used with a reflexive pronoun — meaning you are keeping yourself entertained:

  • "He amused himself by reading comic books all afternoon."
  • "The children amused themselves in the garden."
  • "She amused herself with crossword puzzles during the wait."

This use is simply about finding something pleasant to do with your time, especially when there is nothing else going on.
A Subtle but Important Nuance: The Slightly Detached Tone

"Amused" can sometimes carry a faintly superior or detached quality — as if the person being amused is watching something from a calm, elevated distance, and finds it gently funny because it is a little naive, innocent, or unwittingly ridiculous.

  • "The professor was amused by the student's confident but wrong answer."

The professor doesn't burst out laughing. He finds it mildly funny in a quiet, knowing way.

  • "She was amused by his attempts to seem impressive."

She is not mocking him — but she finds his effort a little cute and quietly funny.

This does not make "amused" a mean or unkind word. It simply means the feeling can include a hint of gentle irony — the awareness that something is funny precisely because of how simple, innocent, or unknowing it is. Think of a parent watching a toddler try to be very serious — that warm, gentle, slightly knowing smile is "amusement."

• It does not mean to strongly excite or thrill someone.
  • It does not mean to impress someone.
  • It does not mean to move someone deeply or emotionally.
  • It does not mean to make someone laugh loudly or hysterically — those require phrases like "cracked everyone up" or "had them in stitches."
  • It is not the same as "bemuse." This is a very common confusion. Bemuse means to puzzle, confuse, or bewilder someone. Amuse means to entertain or make someone smile. They look similar but mean very different things.

Knowing the whole word family will make you much more confident:

Amused (adjective) — describes the person feeling the gentle pleasure.
"She had an amused look on her face." / "He seemed amused by the whole situation."

Amusing (adjective) — describes the thing that causes the amusement.
"That was an amusing story." / "He made an amusing observation."

Amusement (noun) — the feeling itself, or something that provides entertainment.
"I watched in amusement as the cat chased its own tail." / "The fair offered many amusements for children."

Amusingly (adverb) — in a way that amuses.
"He described the embarrassing incident amusingly."

To amuse is to cause someone to feel mild pleasure, gentle humor, or light entertainment. It is a warm, easy feeling — the kind that makes you smile quietly rather than burst out laughing. You can amuse other people, or you can amuse yourself by staying pleasantly busy. Occasionally, it carries a faint sense of knowing, detached irony — finding something sweetly funny because it is a little naive. The word never suggests intense excitement, deep emotion, or loud laughter. It belongs firmly in the gentle, comfortable territory of quiet, pleasant enjoyment.
695:
When you feel amused, you are experiencing a gentle, pleasant feeling of finding something funny or entertaining. It is a light, comfortable, relaxed kind of enjoyment — the kind that makes you smile quietly or let out a soft chuckle. Think of it as a warm, easy feeling that sits somewhere between a slight smile and a soft laugh.

It is important to understand right away that "amused" describes a mild feeling. It is not intense. It is not loud. If something makes you amused, you are pleasantly entertained — but you are not rolling on the floor laughing.
What It Actually Feels Like

Imagine you are watching a small child try very seriously to tie their shoes, failing again and again with a frustrated little face. You are not laughing loudly at them. You are not bored. You are simply watching with a warm, gentle enjoyment — a small smile on your face, feeling softly entertained. That is what being amused feels like.

Or imagine a friend tries to tell a joke but completely messes up the punchline. You are not crying with laughter, but something about it makes you smile and feel lightly entertained. You are amused.
What It Looks Like From the Outside

Because "amused" is a feeling on the inside, it usually shows up on the outside in small, gentle ways:

  • A quiet smile or a knowing grin
  • A soft chuckle (a gentle, restrained laugh)
  • Eyes that look bright or slightly playful
  • A relaxed, comfortable expression

You will often see "amused" used to describe someone's expression, look, or tone — for example, an amused smile, an amused look, an amused tone of voice.
A Very Important Nuance: Mild Superiority

Here is something subtle but important that many learners miss. "Amused" sometimes carries a very gentle sense of feeling slightly above the situation — like you are an observer who finds something funny in a calm, detached way, while the other person is unaware.

For example: if your boss makes a silly spelling mistake in a company email, and you notice it and quietly smile to yourself, you are amused. You are not angry. You are not laughing out loud. You are simply in a position where you can see the humor in the situation gently and comfortably, with a slight sense of "I noticed something others might not have."

This is not mockery. It is not cruel. It is simply a quiet, comfortable enjoyment that sometimes comes with a gentle sense of being one step above the moment.
Where "Amused" Sits on the Scale

It helps to see where "amused" sits compared to other feelings:

Bored → Mildly interested → Amused → Entertained → Laughing → Hysterical

"Amused" lives on the lighter, gentler end. It is never overwhelming. It never takes over your whole body. It is always calm and easy.
What "Amused" Is NOT

Understanding what a word is not is just as important as knowing what it is.

Amused is not the same as:

  • Hilarious / hysterical / in stitches — those describe intense, uncontrollable laughter. Amused is far softer.
  • Excited — excitement is energetic and forward-moving. Amusement is relaxed and observational.
  • Happy — happiness is broad and general. Amusement is specifically about finding something entertaining or funny in a light way.
  • Impressed — being impressed means recognizing someone's skill or achievement. Being amused means finding something gently funny or entertaining.
  • Delighted — delight is a stronger, warmer happiness. Amusement is quieter.
  • Annoyed — this is the opposite. If something annoys you, it bothers you. If it amuses you, it pleasantly entertains you.
The Famous Phrase: "I Am Not Amused"

There is a very well-known English expression — "I am not amused" — which means: I do not find this funny at all. I am displeased. It is often said in a serious, firm, slightly cold tone. It is the direct opposite of being amused.

This phrase is closely associated with Queen Victoria of England, who was said to have used it when someone tried to entertain her with something she found inappropriate or unfunny. Today, people use this phrase — sometimes humorously — when they want to make it very clear that they are not entertained.

Knowing this phrase helps you understand the word better: being amused means exactly what this phrase denies — a genuine, gentle feeling of being entertained or finding something funny.
How "Amused" Is Used With Other Words

In real English, "amused" very commonly appears in these patterns:

  • Amused by something — "She was amused by his terrible dancing."
  • Amused at something — "He was amused at the irony of the situation."
  • Amused smile / look / expression / grin — describing how the amusement appears on someone's face.
  • Amused tone — the way someone speaks when they find something gently funny.
  • Quietly / mildly / clearly amused — these adverbs are very natural with "amused" because they match its gentle nature.
  • Keep someone / yourself amused — to find ways to stay entertained. "She kept herself amused during the long flight by reading."
Example Sentences

Here are sentences showing the word in different real-life situations:

  1. The professor listened to the student's very wrong but very confident answer, wearing an amused smile.

(The professor found it gently funny but did not mock the student.)

  1. He was amused by the way the cat kept falling off the couch and immediately pretending it had meant to do that.

(Light, warm entertainment at something funny and harmless.)

  1. She looked mildly amused when her husband tried to assemble the furniture without reading the instructions.

(A gentle, knowing amusement — she could see what was coming.)

  1. "I am not amused," said the manager, when the team spent the whole meeting making jokes instead of working.

(Not entertained — in fact, displeased.)

  1. The children's attempts to bake a cake kept the grandparents amused all afternoon.

(Gently entertained over a period of time — a comfortable, enjoyable feeling.)

  1. There was an amused glint in her eyes as she listened to his excuse.

(Her eyes showed that quiet, knowing enjoyment — she saw the humor but kept it mostly inside.)
The Word Family

Since you want a complete understanding, here are the closely related words:

  • To amuse (verb): to cause someone to feel amused. The thing or person that entertains you is what amuses you. "The comedian amused the crowd." / "His clumsiness amused her."
  • Amusement (noun): the feeling itself, or something that entertains you. "She watched with amusement." / "The fair had many amusements for children."
  • Amusing (adjective): this describes the thing that causes amusement — not the person feeling it. "The story was amusing." (The story caused amusement.) Compare: "She was amused by the story." (She felt amusement.)
  • Unamused: simply means not amused — not entertained, possibly annoyed or indifferent.

A quick way to keep amusing and amused separate: the thing is amusing; the person is amused. "The joke was amusing. He was amused by the joke."
The Full Picture in One Paragraph

To bring it all together: amused describes a gentle, light, pleasant feeling of finding something entertaining or funny in a relaxed, comfortable way. It shows up as a quiet smile, a soft chuckle, or a bright look in the eyes. It is never intense or overwhelming. It sometimes carries a very subtle sense of calm, observational enjoyment — like watching something from a pleasant distance. It is the opposite of being bored, annoyed, or unentertained. And whenever you hear someone say "I am not amused," know that they are deliberately rejecting this feeling — signaling displeasure, not gentle enjoyment.
696:
"An arm and a leg" means a very large amount of money — so much that it feels unreasonably or shockingly expensive. When something "costs an arm and a leg," it means it is extremely expensive.

The idea behind it is simple and powerful: your arms and legs are among the most valuable things you have. They are a part of your body. You cannot buy them or replace them. So if you had to pay with an arm and a leg, that would be the highest price imaginable. The idiom uses this dramatic image to say: "This thing costs so much, it feels like I'm giving up something truly precious."

This idiom is almost always used with verbs related to money and paying. The most common patterns are:

  • cost an arm and a leg → "That car costs an arm and a leg."
  • pay an arm and a leg → "I paid an arm and a leg for this jacket."
  • charge an arm and a leg → "That mechanic charges an arm and a leg."
  • spend an arm and a leg → "We spent an arm and a leg on the wedding."

Here are clear examples showing how native speakers actually use it:

  • "Good coffee in that café is great, but it costs an arm and a leg."
  • "Healthcare in some countries costs an arm and a leg if you don't have insurance."
  • "She wanted to buy a designer handbag, but they were charging an arm and a leg."
  • "We didn't go to Paris in the summer because flights cost an arm and a leg."
  • "The plumber fixed the leak in ten minutes but charged us an arm and a leg."

This is important: "an arm and a leg" does not mean just "a little expensive" or "pricier than usual." It means something feels shockingly, unreasonably, or frustratingly expensive. There is almost always a sense of surprise or complaint behind it.

Think of it on a scale like this:

  • Slightly expensive → "a bit pricey"
  • Noticeably expensive → "pretty expensive"
  • Very expensive → "costs a fortune"
  • Shockingly, outrageously expensive → "costs an arm and a leg" ✅

So you would probably not say a $3 coffee costs an arm and a leg. But you might say a $15 coffee costs an arm and a leg. It depends on context and what feels unreasonable to the speaker.
The Tone and Feeling Behind It

When someone uses this idiom, they are almost always expressing one of these feelings:

  • Complaint: "That hotel cost us an arm and a leg — never going back."
  • Warning: "Be careful with that mechanic. He charges an arm and a leg."
  • Surprise or shock: "Can you believe it? A simple sandwich cost an arm and a leg at the airport."
  • Frustration: "I'd love a new laptop, but good ones cost an arm and a leg."

It is rarely used in a neutral or positive way. It almost always carries a negative emotional weight.

This idiom is informal and conversational. You will hear it in everyday speech between friends, family, and colleagues. You might also see it in casual writing, like blogs, social media, or opinion articles.

You would not use it in formal writing, such as a business report, academic essay, or official letter. In those cases, you would simply say "at a significant cost," "at a high price," or "expensive."

The exact origin is not 100% confirmed, but the most widely accepted explanation among language historians connects it to the idea of sacrifice and war.

In battles, soldiers sometimes lost their arms and legs — the most devastating physical sacrifice a person could make. Over time, the phrase "giving an arm and a leg" grew to mean paying the ultimate price or making the greatest possible sacrifice. Eventually, this idea moved into everyday language and became attached to money: if something costs you an arm and a leg, it's as though you are sacrificing something of the greatest possible value to get it.

There is a popular but likely false story that the idiom comes from portrait painters in the 1600s and 1700s, who supposedly charged extra to paint a person's arms and legs in a portrait. However, language historians find no evidence of this, and the phrase itself does not appear in written records until the 1940s and 1950s in American English — long after the age of formal portrait painting. So the wartime sacrifice theory is far more credible.
Similar Idioms That Mean the Same Thing

English has several other idioms that also mean "very expensive." Knowing them helps you understand the range of expression around this idea:

  • "Cost a fortune" → "That surgery cost a fortune."
  • "Cost a pretty penny" → "That ring must have cost a pretty penny."
  • "Break the bank" → "A weekend trip doesn't have to break the bank."
  • "Doesn't come cheap" → "Quality furniture doesn't come cheap."

Among all of these, "costs an arm and a leg" is one of the most vivid and emotionally charged because of the physical image it creates.

Mistake 1: Using it for things that are only slightly expensive.
This idiom is for things that feel outrageously expensive. Using it for something only mildly pricey sounds like an overreaction.

Mistake 2: Changing the body parts.
The idiom is fixed. You cannot say "costs an arm and a hand" or "costs a leg and a foot." It is always specifically an arm and a leg.

Mistake 3: Using it in formal writing.
Stick to formal vocabulary in professional or academic contexts.

"An arm and a leg" = extremely expensive, to a shocking or frustrating degree. It is an informal expression, used to complain about or warn others about a very high price. It paints a dramatic picture — as if you are paying with parts of your own body — to show just how valuable (and painful!) the cost feels.
697:
An open secret is something that is supposed to be a secret — but in reality, almost everyone already knows about it. The people involved may still treat it as a secret officially, but the information has quietly spread around until it's common knowledge.

Think of it this way: a regular secret is hidden. An open secret is a secret in name only — the hiding is just a performance at this point.
Why It Sounds Like a Contradiction

At first glance, "open" and "secret" seem like complete opposites. How can something be both open and secret? That's exactly the point. The idiom is intentionally contradictory, because it describes an ironic situation — something that carries the label of a secret, while functioning as public knowledge in practice.

This kind of expression is called an oxymoron (a phrase combining two opposite ideas). The tension between the two words is what gives the idiom its punch and meaning.
A Simple, Concrete Example

Imagine a couple at your workplace. They are dating, but they haven't officially told anyone. However, everyone in the office has noticed them arriving together, leaving together, and exchanging glances all day. Nobody is supposed to know — but everybody does.

Their relationship is an open secret.

Nobody talks about it openly (or maybe they do, just not in front of the couple), but the "secret" has completely failed at being a secret.
The Key Ingredients

For something to qualify as an open secret, it needs three things:

  1. An intention to keep it hidden. Someone — a person, a company, a government — wants the information to stay private, or at least acts like they do.
  2. Widespread awareness despite that intention. The information is already known by many, most, or all of the people in a relevant group.
  3. A lack of official acknowledgment. Nobody publicly admits or confirms it, even though everyone knows. There's a kind of collective pretending going on.

All three ingredients together create the unique, slightly absurd situation that the idiom captures.
The Tone and Feel of This Idiom

"An open secret" often carries a slightly ironic, sometimes cynical tone. It hints that:

  • Someone's attempt at secrecy has failed — perhaps embarrassingly so.
  • There is a gap between official reality and actual reality. What is said publicly and what people actually know are two different things.
  • People are playing along with a fiction. Everyone knows, but for various social, political, or professional reasons, nobody formally says so.

Because of this, the idiom often shows up in contexts that involve a light criticism or a knowing observation about human behavior — the way people pretend not to know things, or the way institutions pretend not to do things.
Real-World Contexts Where This Idiom Appears

In the workplace:
"It's an open secret that the company is planning to lay off staff — everyone's been updating their résumés."

In politics:
"His ambition to run for president is an open secret — he's been quietly building his campaign team for months."

In entertainment/celebrity culture:
"Their on-set romance was an open secret long before they confirmed it in interviews."

In everyday social situations:
"It's an open secret in our family that grandma doesn't actually like the cake she bakes — she makes it because we love it."

In business and finance:
"The company's accounting problems were an open secret among insiders, even as executives denied any issues publicly."
What Keeps an Open Secret "Alive" as a Secret?

This is a fascinating part of the idiom. If everyone knows, why is it still called a secret? Because the official denial or silence remains in place. People may:

  • Fear the social consequences of being the one to say it out loud.
  • Respect an unspoken social agreement not to address it directly.
  • Lack formal proof, even though informal knowledge is widespread.
  • Not want to embarrass the person or organization involved.
  • Simply find it more comfortable or politically safer to look the other way.

An open secret survives because of collective silence, even in the face of collective knowledge.
How It Is Different from Related Concepts

ConceptMeaning
A secretKnown only to very few; genuinely hidden.
An open secretKnown to many, but not officially acknowledged.
GossipUnofficial information that is actively being spread and discussed.
Public knowledgeFully acknowledged, confirmed, and freely discussable.

An open secret sits in the uncomfortable middle ground — past "secret," but never quite reaching "public knowledge." It is in a kind of limbo.
The Origin of the Phrase

The concept is very old. In Italian, there is a phrase — il segreto di Pulcinella — meaning "Pulcinella's secret," referring to a stock comic character from traditional Italian theater (Commedia dell'arte) who would "whisper" something to the audience while the other characters pretended not to hear. Everyone knew. The character still called it a secret. The humor came from the absurdity of the fiction.

In English, the phrase "open secret" has been in use since at least the early 19th century, appearing in literature and journalism over the years. The playwright Alfred de Musset used the equivalent French phrase as a play title (Un secret de Polichinelle) in 1824. In English, Lord Tennyson and other 19th-century writers used the phrase, and it has been common in the language ever since.
How to Use It Correctly

✅ Correct usage — use it when referring to something widely known but not officially confirmed or spoken about:

  • "It's an open secret that she's the one who actually runs the department."
  • "The merger was an open secret months before the official announcement."

❌ Incorrect usage — don't use it for something that is genuinely unknown or truly private:

  • "Nobody knows what she keeps in that box — it's an open secret." ← This is wrong, because if nobody knows, it's just a regular secret.
One-Sentence Summary to Lock It In

An open secret is something that is officially a secret, but practically speaking, everyone already knows about it — and the "secrecy" is little more than a polite fiction that no one openly challenges.

Once you understand this idiom, you'll start noticing it everywhere — in news articles, conversations, books, and films. It is one of those phrases that perfectly captures a very specific and very human tendency: our remarkable ability to collectively pretend we don't know something we absolutely all know.
698:
An anachronism is something — an object, a word, a custom, a technology, a person, or an idea — that appears in the wrong time period. It doesn't belong to the era it's associated with. The word always signals a mismatch between something and the time in which it appears.

The simplest way to hold the meaning: an anachronism is a thing out of its time.

Imagine watching a movie set in ancient Rome. A Roman soldier reaches into his toga and pulls out a smartphone. That smartphone is an anachronism. It belongs to our century, not to ancient Rome. It has been placed in a time where it could not possibly have existed.

Or picture a historical novel set in 1800s England where characters casually mention streaming a show on Netflix. That reference is an anachronism — Netflix didn't exist in the 1800s, and placing it there creates a jarring time-mismatch.

Most people assume an anachronism is always something too new showing up in a time too old — like the smartphone in Rome. That is by far the most common kind. But it can also work in reverse: something too old appearing in a context too new. A realistic war film set today, where soldiers fight exclusively with medieval swords and crossbows, would contain anachronisms in that direction.

Both qualify because both involve the same essential error: something is temporally displaced, placed outside the era it belongs to.

This distinction matters a great deal.

Unintentional anachronisms are mistakes, usually errors of research. A filmmaker sets a scene in 1940 but dresses an actor in a style of suit that wasn't fashionable until 1962. That's an accidental anachronism — a slip in historical accuracy. Historians, costume experts, and eagle-eyed viewers love spotting these. Famous examples exist in big-budget films: a wristwatch glimpsed on a Roman soldier in a period epic, a modern jet trail visible in the sky of a Civil War scene.

Intentional anachronisms are deliberate creative choices. A playwright might set a tragedy in ancient Athens but have the characters speak in modern slang — on purpose — to make the audience feel how universal and timeless certain human experiences are. A novelist might drop a reference to something modern into a Victorian story to create a humorous or thought-provoking contrast. When used this way, anachronism becomes a literary and theatrical device, not an error.

Anachronism isn't limited to objects or references. It can describe a person too. If someone dresses, thinks, and lives as though they are from a completely different era, you might call them an anachronism — they feel out of step with the present moment, as if they accidentally wandered in from another century.

"He's a lovable anachronism — in the age of instant messaging, he still writes long letters by hand and seals them with wax."

This usage is often affectionate, sometimes critical, but always carries that same core idea: this person doesn't quite fit the time they're living in.
When It Describes Ideas, Laws, or Institutions

Anachronism is also commonly used to describe ideas, customs, laws, or institutions that have outlived their era. When a rule written for a completely different world is still being enforced today, people call it an anachronism — meaning it made sense once, but now it belongs to a time that has passed.

"That law is an anachronism — it was designed for a world without the internet and has no place in modern society."

This usage carries a slightly critical edge. To call something an anachronism in this sense is to suggest it should perhaps be retired, updated, or at least questioned.

Seeing a word in action cements it. Here are varied examples across different contexts:

"The armor in that battle scene was a glaring anachronism — that particular style wasn't developed until two centuries after the story takes place."

"The director deliberately filled the film with anachronisms, mixing medieval costumes with modern dialogue, to blur the line between then and now."

"Some argue that the monarchy is an anachronism in a modern democracy."

"The word she used was an anachronism — it didn't enter the English language until long after the time the novel is set."

"With his old-fashioned manners and formal way of speaking, he's something of a charming anachronism at the office."

Since you want to know this word fully, here are the forms you'll encounter:

Anachronistic is the adjective form. You use it to describe something that is an anachronism. "The rotary phone on his desk looked anachronistic next to everyone else's laptops."

Anachronistically is the adverb form. "The film was anachronistically scored with 1980s pop music despite being set in the 1940s."
The One Thing to Lock In

Every time you encounter "anachronism," your brain should immediately fire on the word time and the idea of mismatch. Something is where — or rather when — it shouldn't be. It's either too early or too late. The error or device is always about time specifically, not about place, style, or logic in a general sense. Time is the whole point. Fix that anchor and the word will never confuse you again.
699:
Anachronistic describes something that is out of place in time — it exists in, or is used in, a time period where it simply does not belong.

Think of it this way: everything in the world has a "home" in time. A smartphone belongs to the 21st century. A horse-drawn carriage belongs to the 18th century. When something shows up in the wrong era — whether too early or too late — it becomes anachronistic. It's a temporal mismatch, a collision between an object, idea, word, or custom and the time period surrounding it.
The Two Main Situations Where You'll See This Word

1. A Historical Error (Something Appearing Too Early)

This is the classic use. When a film, novel, or play is set in a specific historical period, and something appears in it that didn't exist yet at that time, that thing is anachronistic.

Imagine watching a movie set in ancient Rome, and a soldier is wearing a wristwatch. The wristwatch is anachronistic — it belongs to the 20th century, not ancient Rome. It's a glaring error of time.

More examples:

  • A character in a 16th-century story sends a text message → anachronistic.
  • A painting of Napoleon holding a plastic bottle of water → anachronistic.
  • A Shakespeare play where a character mentions the internet → anachronistic.

In all these cases, something modern has been placed in a historical setting where it couldn't possibly have existed. The thing is wrong for its time.

2. Something Outdated in a Modern Context (Something Belonging to the Past)

You'll also hear "anachronistic" used to describe something that still exists today but feels like it belongs to a much earlier era — as if it got left behind when time moved forward.

Examples:

  • A company in 2026 that still uses fax machines exclusively, when email and instant messaging exist → their communication system is anachronistic.
  • A law written in 1750 that still hasn't been updated and no longer makes sense in modern society → it's anachronistic.
  • A teacher who forbids students from using any technology and insists on memorizing encyclopedias → an anachronistic teaching method.

In these cases, nothing is placed in a historical film or story — the thing genuinely exists right now. But it belongs to another time. It's a relic. It hasn't kept pace with the era it now lives in.
The Thread That Connects Both Uses

Whether it's a smartphone in ancient Rome or a fax machine in 2026, the feeling is the same: something is mismatched with its time. It either arrived too early (before its time), or it overstayed its welcome (past its time). That mismatch — that friction between a thing and the era it occupies — is what "anachronistic" captures.

It's not the same as simply "old." An ancient Egyptian scroll displayed in a museum is not anachronistic — it belongs there, in context, because we understand its historical place. But if a character in a film set in ancient Egypt pulls out a scroll that was clearly printed on a modern laser printer, that is anachronistic. Age alone doesn't make something anachronistic. The mismatch does.

It can be a mistake or a deliberate choice. A director might accidentally show a modern car in the background of a period film — an unintentional anachronism. But another director might purposely mix eras for artistic effect, like dressing medieval knights in modern suits. In both cases the word applies, but the intent is different.

The tone of the word is flexible. It can be critical ("that law is anachronistic and needs to go"), neutral ("the film contains several anachronistic details"), or even gently admiring ("he runs his bakery in an anachronistic, almost romantic way — everything made entirely by hand").

• Anachronism (noun) — the thing itself that is out of place in time. "That wristwatch in the Roman film is a glaring anachronism."
  • Anachronistic (adjective) — describes something as being out of place in time. "The wristwatch looked completely anachronistic."
  • Anachronistically (adverb) — describes how something is done in an out-of-time way. "The office was anachronistically decorated with rotary phones and typewriters."
A One-Line Summary to Lock It In

Anachronistic = belonging to the wrong time period.

If you see a caveman using a microwave, or a 2026 courtroom that still uses quill pens and candlelight, your instinct to say "that doesn't fit the time" — that instinct has a precise, elegant word: anachronistic.
